---
title: "Comparing models"
description: "Is one model really better, or did the test set favour it by chance? Paired bootstrap, DeLong's test for AUC and the Diebold–Mariano test for losses."
---

```{python}
#| include: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from modelperf.data import FEATURES, train_test
from modelperf.metrics import (
    auc_rank,
    bootstrap_summary,
    delong_test,
    diebold_mariano,
    gini_index,
    paired_bootstrap,
    tweedie_deviance,
)
from modelperf.models import TWEEDIE_POWER, binary_predictions, load_models, pure_premium_predictions
from modelperf.plots import plot_intervals, plot_paired_bootstrap, use_style

use_style()
b = binary_predictions()
y = b["y"].to_numpy()
auc = {m: auc_rank(y, b[m]) for m in ("GLM", "GBM")}
N_BOOT = 1000


def fmt_p(p):
    return "< 0.001" if p < 0.001 else f"{p:.3f}"


def comparison_table(results: dict, digits: str = ".4g") -> pd.DataFrame:
    """One row per comparison: difference, standard error, 95% interval, p-value."""
    t = pd.DataFrame(results).T
    return pd.DataFrame({
        "difference": t["difference"].map(f"{{:{digits}}}".format),
        "std. error": t["std. error"].map(f"{{:{digits}}}".format),
        "95% interval": [f"[{lo:{digits}}, {hi:{digits}}]" for lo, hi in zip(t["lower"], t["upper"])],
        "p-value": t["p-value"].map(fmt_p),
    })
```

**Question answered:** is one model really better than another, or did the
test set happen to favour it?

Every metric on the earlier pages was computed on one test set of
`{python} f"{len(y):,}"` policies. A different sample of policies would have
given slightly different values, so each metric is an *estimate* with sampling
uncertainty. When two models are close, the question is whether their gap is
larger than that uncertainty. This page covers three ways to answer it:

- the **paired bootstrap**, which works for any metric;
- **DeLong's test**, a fast formula for the difference between two AUCs;
- the **Diebold–Mariano test**, for any metric that is an average of
  per-observation losses (log loss, Brier score, deviance).

It ends by settling a question left open on the
[lift chart page](../continuous/lift-lorenz.qmd): is the GLM–GBM blend's
improvement real?

## Compare the difference, not two intervals

Both models are scored on the **same** policies. That matters: a test set that
happens to contain many easy-to-rank policies flatters *both* models at once.
Most of the sampling noise is shared, and it cancels in the difference.

The tempting shortcut, computing an interval for each model and checking
whether they overlap, ignores this. It treats the two estimates as independent
and overstates the uncertainty of the difference, often by a large factor. The
right approach measures the uncertainty of the **difference itself**, on paired
data. All three methods below do that.

## The paired bootstrap

The bootstrap estimates sampling uncertainty by imitating the sampling:

1. draw a **resample** of the test set: as many policies as it has, drawn at
   random *with replacement* (some appear twice, others not at all);
2. score **both models on the same resample** and record their difference;
3. repeat many times (here `{python} f"{N_BOOT:,}"`).

The spread of the recorded differences shows how much the difference would
vary from one test set to another. Its 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles give a 95%
**percentile interval**.

Here is the AUC of the two `HasClaim` models from the
[ROC page](../binary/roc-auc.qmd):

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
boot = paired_bootstrap(auc_rank, y, {m: b[m] for m in ("GLM", "GBM")}, n_boot=N_BOOT)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-bootstrap-auc
#| fig-cap: "Paired bootstrap of the AUC on the test set. Left: GBM against GLM AUC, one point per resample. Right: distribution of the difference GBM − GLM, with its 95% percentile interval shaded."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.4))
plot_paired_bootstrap(boot, "GBM", "GLM", axes)
fig.tight_layout()
```

```{python}
#| include: false
diff = boot["GBM"] - boot["GLM"]
boot_auc = bootstrap_summary(auc["GBM"] - auc["GLM"], diff)
se = boot.std()
unpaired_se = np.sqrt(se["GLM"] ** 2 + se["GBM"] ** 2)
corr = boot["GLM"].corr(boot["GBM"])
```

The left panel shows why pairing matters. From one resample to the next, the
AUCs move together (correlation `{python} f"{corr:.2f}"`): a resample that is
easy for the GLM is easy for the GBM too. Each AUC on its own has a standard
error of about `{python} f"{se.mean():.4f}"`, but their difference only
`{python} f"{boot_auc['std. error']:.4f}"`. Treating the models as independent
would give `{python} f"{unpaired_se:.4f}"`, overstating the uncertainty
`{python} f"{unpaired_se / boot_auc['std. error']:.1f}"` times.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bootstrap-auc
#| tbl-cap: "AUC of each model and of their difference, with bootstrap standard errors and 95% percentile intervals."
pd.DataFrame({
    **{m: {"AUC": auc[m], "std. error": se[m], "lower": boot[m].quantile(0.025), "upper": boot[m].quantile(0.975)}
       for m in ("GLM", "GBM")},
    "GBM − GLM": boot_auc.rename({"difference": "AUC"}).drop("p-value"),
}).T.round(4)
```

The whole interval for GBM − GLM lies above 0: not one of the
`{python} f"{N_BOOT:,}"` resamples had the GLM ahead. The GBM ranks better,
and not by chance.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why the bootstrap works, and when it doesn't
The bootstrap treats the test set as a stand-in for the population and
resamples from it. It works for any metric you can compute, however
complicated (AUC, Gini, a lift ratio, the precision in the top 5%), which makes
it the default tool. It needs:

- **Independent observations.** Resampling single policies assumes each is a
  separate draw. With grouped data (several policies per customer) or time
  series, resample whole groups or blocks instead.
- **Enough resamples.** 1,000 is plenty for a 95% interval. Small p-values
  need more: with B resamples a p-value can't go much below 2/B.
- **Time.** Every resample recomputes the metric for every model.
:::

## DeLong's test for AUC

For AUC there is a formula that gives the same answer without resampling.
DeLong, DeLong and Clarke-Pearson (1988) start from the reading of AUC on the
[ROC page](../binary/roc-auc.qmd): the share of (claim, no-claim) pairs that
the model orders correctly. That share is an average over pairs, so it splits
into a contribution per policy, its **placement value**:

- for a policy **with** a claim: the share of no-claim policies it outscores;
- for a policy **without** a claim: the share of claim policies that outscore it

(ties count ½). Both sets of placement values average to the AUC, and their
variances give the variance of the AUC. For two models, the same computation
on the **per-policy differences** of their placement values gives the variance
of the AUC difference, with the pairing built in:

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\text{AUC}}_A - \widehat{\text{AUC}}_B)
= \frac{\operatorname{Var}(V^A_{1} - V^B_{1})}{n_1}
+ \frac{\operatorname{Var}(V^A_{0} - V^B_{0})}{n_0},
$$

where $V_1$ are the placement values of the $n_1$ claim policies and $V_0$
those of the $n_0$ no-claim policies. The test statistic is the difference
divided by its standard error, compared with the normal distribution.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-delong
#| tbl-cap: "AUC of GBM − GLM: DeLong's test and the paired bootstrap."
#| code-fold: false
delong = delong_test(y, b["GBM"], b["GLM"])
comparison_table({"DeLong": delong, "Paired bootstrap": boot_auc})
```

The two methods agree closely: DeLong's standard error is
`{python} f"{delong['std. error']:.5f}"`, the bootstrap's
`{python} f"{boot_auc['std. error']:.5f}"`. DeLong's p-value can go far below
anything 1,000 resamples could show, and it takes a fraction of a second. For
AUC alone, DeLong is the standard choice. For other metrics, use the
bootstrap.

## The Diebold–Mariano test for losses

Log loss, the Brier score, squared error and deviance are all **averages of a
loss per observation**. Comparing two models on such a metric is comparing two
averages over the same observations. Diebold and Mariano (1995) test this
through the **loss differential** of each observation,

$$
d_i = L(y_i, \hat y^A_i) - L(y_i, \hat y^B_i),
$$

whose average is the difference in the metric. If the models are equally good,
the $d_i$ average to 0 apart from noise. The test divides $\bar d$ by its
standard error, $\text{sd}(d) / \sqrt n$, and compares the result with the
normal distribution. With weights (such as exposure) both the average and its
standard error are weighted.

For independent observations this is simply a **paired test** on the losses.
The name comes from forecasting, where the observations form a time series:
there the standard error must allow for autocorrelation between consecutive
$d_i$ (a Newey–West standard error), which is the original test's real
contribution.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-dm-binary
#| tbl-cap: "Diebold–Mariano tests for HasClaim: GLM loss − GBM loss (positive means the GBM is better)."
#| code-fold: false
p_glm, p_gbm = b["GLM"].to_numpy(), b["GBM"].to_numpy()
log_loss_per_policy = lambda p: -(y * np.log(p) + (1 - y) * np.log(1 - p))
comparison_table({
    "log loss": diebold_mariano(log_loss_per_policy(p_glm), log_loss_per_policy(p_gbm)),
    "Brier score": diebold_mariano((p_glm - y) ** 2, (p_gbm - y) ** 2),
})
```

```{python}
#| include: false
dm_ll = diebold_mariano(log_loss_per_policy(p_glm), log_loss_per_policy(p_gbm))
ll_glm = np.mean(log_loss_per_policy(p_glm))
```

The GBM's log loss is `{python} f"{dm_ll['difference'] / ll_glm:.1%}"` lower
than the GLM's, a small relative gain but measured very precisely: on a large
test set even small differences in an average loss are easy to detect. The
probabilities agree with the ranking from the AUC tests. The GBM is better on
both.

Two things the Diebold–Mariano test can't do:

- **AUC and Gini are not averages of per-observation losses.** They depend on
  pairs or on the ranking of the whole test set, so they have no loss
  differential. Use DeLong or the bootstrap.
- **It compares scores, not truth.** A significant difference in log loss
  says one model's probabilities are closer to the outcomes on average. It
  says nothing about *where*: for that, look at calibration plots and double
  lift charts.

## Is the blend's improvement real?

The [lift chart page](../continuous/lift-lorenz.qmd) found that the GLM and the
GBM for pure premium each detect mispricing in the other, and that their
geometric mean beats both. But all three Gini indices lay within about 0.015
of each other, on a target where a few large claims dominate everything. Time
to test.

One detail first. On the lift chart page, the blend was rescaled so that its
average on the **test set** matched the actual average. That uses the test
outcomes, which would flatter the blend's deviance. Here the scale factor
comes from the training set, so nothing about the blend is fitted on the test
data. (The Gini doesn't depend on the scale, so it is unchanged.)

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
pp = pure_premium_predictions()
yp, w = pp["y"].to_numpy(), pp["w"].to_numpy()

train, fitted = train_test().train, load_models()["pure_premium"]
glm_train, gbm_train = (fitted[m].predict(train[FEATURES]) for m in ("GLM", "GBM"))
scale = np.average(train["PurePremium"], weights=train["Exposure"]) / np.average(
    np.sqrt(glm_train * gbm_train), weights=train["Exposure"]
)
scores = {m: pp[m].to_numpy() for m in ("GLM", "GBM")}
scores["Blend"] = scale * np.sqrt(scores["GLM"] * scores["GBM"])
```

We compare all three pairs on two metrics:

- the **Gini index**, a ranking metric with no per-policy loss: paired
  bootstrap, resampling policies together with their exposure;
- **D²**, the share of the Null model's Tweedie deviance explained: the
  Diebold–Mariano test on the per-policy deviance, weighted by exposure. Since
  all models share the same Null deviance, a difference in D² is a difference
  in mean deviance divided by the Null deviance.

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
pairs = [("GBM", "GLM"), ("Blend", "GLM"), ("Blend", "GBM")]
gini = {m: gini_index(yp, s, w) for m, s in scores.items()}
gini_boot = paired_bootstrap(gini_index, yp, scores, w, n_boot=N_BOOT)
gini_tests = {f"{a} − {c}": bootstrap_summary(gini[a] - gini[c], gini_boot[a] - gini_boot[c]) for a, c in pairs}

deviance = {m: tweedie_deviance(yp, s, TWEEDIE_POWER) for m, s in scores.items()}
null_deviance = np.average(tweedie_deviance(yp, pp["Null"], TWEEDIE_POWER), weights=w)
d2_tests = {}
for a, c in pairs:
    dm = diebold_mariano(deviance[c], deviance[a], w)  # positive: model a has lower deviance
    scaled = ["difference", "std. error", "lower", "upper"]
    d2_tests[f"{a} − {c}"] = pd.concat([dm[scaled] / null_deviance, dm[["p-value"]]])
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-blend-intervals
#| fig-cap: "Differences in Gini index (paired bootstrap) and D² (Diebold–Mariano) between the pure premium models, with 95% intervals. An interval crossing 0 is compatible with no difference."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.2), sharey=True)
plot_intervals(pd.DataFrame(gini_tests).T, ax=axes[0], xlabel="Difference in Gini index", title="Gini (ranking)")
plot_intervals(pd.DataFrame(d2_tests).T, ax=axes[1], xlabel="Difference in D²", title="D² (deviance)")
fig.tight_layout()
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-blend-tests
#| tbl-cap: "Pure premium: differences between the models, test set."
pd.concat({"Gini (bootstrap)": comparison_table(gini_tests, ".3f"),
           "D² (Diebold–Mariano)": comparison_table(d2_tests, ".4f")}, axis=1)
```

```{python}
#| include: false
g, d = pd.DataFrame(gini_tests).T, pd.DataFrame(d2_tests).T
gini_se = gini_boot.std()
# How concentrated is the evidence? Share of the differential's variance from the top 0.1% of policies.
diff_dev = deviance["GBM"] - deviance["Blend"]
contrib = np.sort(w**2 * (diff_dev - np.average(diff_dev, weights=w)) ** 2)[::-1]
top_k = int(np.ceil(0.001 * yp.size))
top_share = contrib[:top_k].sum() / contrib.sum()
n_claims = int((yp > 0).sum())
```

Three conclusions, from clear to uncertain:

- **GBM against GLM: no detectable difference.** The Gini difference is
  `{python} f"{g.loc['GBM − GLM', 'difference']:+.3f}"` with an interval from
  `{python} f"{g.loc['GBM − GLM', 'lower']:.3f}"` to
  `{python} f"{g.loc['GBM − GLM', 'upper']:.3f}"`, and the D² difference is
  just as inconclusive (p = `{python} fmt_p(d.loc['GBM − GLM', 'p-value'])`).
  The GBM's clearly better AUC for `HasClaim` does **not** carry over to pure
  premium, where claim sizes add a large amount of noise.
- **Blend against GLM: likely better.** Both intervals exclude 0
  (p = `{python} fmt_p(g.loc['Blend − GLM', 'p-value'])` for the Gini,
  `{python} fmt_p(d.loc['Blend − GLM', 'p-value'])` for D²). That is
  good evidence, though not overwhelming (see the next section).
- **Blend against GBM: suggestive, not established.** Both intervals include
  0: the Gini gain of `{python} f"{g.loc['Blend − GBM', 'difference']:.3f}"`
  has p = `{python} fmt_p(g.loc['Blend − GBM', 'p-value'])`, the D² gain
  p = `{python} fmt_p(d.loc['Blend − GBM', 'p-value'])`.

The pairing is again what makes any of this detectable. Each Gini on its own
has a bootstrap standard error of about `{python} f"{gini_se.mean():.3f}"`, so
the per-model intervals overlap almost completely, yet the blend's difference
from the GLM has a standard error of only
`{python} f"{g.loc['Blend − GLM', 'std. error']:.3f}"`. The blend is built from
the GLM and the GBM, so its ranking is close to both, and most of the noise
cancels.

Why are the intervals so wide? The test set has only
`{python} f"{n_claims:,}"` policies with a claim, and claim costs range over
several orders of magnitude. For the deviance comparison of blend and GBM,
the `{python} f"{top_k:,}"` policies that contribute most (the top 0.1%)
account for `{python} f"{top_share:.0%}"` of the variance of the loss
differential. A handful of large claims decide the result, so the test is far
less precise than the size of the test set suggests.

### Before declaring a winner

**Six tests, not one.** This section ran three comparisons on two metrics.
With six chances, one p-value below 0.05 is less convincing than it looks.
The simplest correction (Bonferroni) asks for p below 0.05 / 6 ≈ 0.008 for
each test, and neither blend result passes it. The blend's gain over the GLM is
still the most credible finding: both metrics point the same way, and the
double lift chart explained *why* blending should help before we tested it.
But it should be confirmed on fresh data before anyone relies on it.

**The blend was suggested by the test set.** We tried it because the double
lift chart, drawn on these same test policies, pointed to it. A 50/50 blend has
no tuned parameter and its scale comes from the training data, so the risk of
having fitted the test set is small. Had we tuned the blend's weight on the
test set, its test-set score would be optimistic and the tests above
invalid. The clean procedure: choose the blend on a validation set, or on
cross-validation folds of the training data, and test once on held-out data.

**Statistical is not practical significance.** A p-value says whether a
difference is distinguishable from noise, not whether it matters. The GBM's
`{python} f"{dm_ll['difference'] / ll_glm:.1%}"` lower log loss is
overwhelmingly significant but may not justify replacing a GLM that regulators
and underwriters understand. Report the **interval for the difference**, and
judge whether its whole range would change a decision.

::: {.callout-note}
## What these tests leave out: the training sample
All three methods resample the **test set**. They answer: 'are these two
*fitted* models different on the population the test set comes from?' That is
the right question when deciding which fitted model to deploy. They ignore that
training on a different sample would have produced different models. To ask
whether one *modelling approach* beats another (GBMs against GLMs in general,
on this kind of data), repeat the fitting across cross-validation folds or
repeated splits, and use a test that accounts for the overlap between training
sets, such as the corrected resampled t-test of Nadeau and Bengio (2003).
:::

## Which test for which metric

| Metric | Average of a loss per observation? | Test |
|---|---|---|
| AUC | no (depends on pairs) | DeLong; or paired bootstrap |
| Gini index, lift ratio, top-k precision | no (depends on the ranking) | paired bootstrap |
| Log loss, Brier score, deviance, MSE, MAE | yes | Diebold–Mariano (paired test on the loss differential); or paired bootstrap |
| D², R² (against the same Null model) | ratio of averages | Diebold–Mariano on the deviance or squared error |
| Any metric, observations over time | — | Diebold–Mariano with a Newey–West standard error; block bootstrap |
| Any metric, grouped observations | — | bootstrap that resamples whole groups |

## Takeaways

- A metric computed on a test set is an **estimate**. Before preferring one
  model, check whether the gap is larger than its sampling uncertainty.
- **Pair the comparison.** Both models are scored on the same observations, so
  test the difference directly. Overlapping per-model intervals say little:
  here the paired standard error was
  `{python} f"{unpaired_se / boot_auc['std. error']:.1f}"` times smaller than the
  unpaired one for AUC.
- The **paired bootstrap** works for any metric. **DeLong's test** gives the
  same answer for AUC instantly. The **Diebold–Mariano test** handles any
  average loss, such as log loss or deviance.
- For `HasClaim`, the GBM beats the GLM beyond doubt. For pure premium, GBM
  and GLM are indistinguishable. The blend is likely better than the GLM
  (p = `{python} fmt_p(g.loc['Blend − GLM', 'p-value'])` and
  `{python} fmt_p(d.loc['Blend − GLM', 'p-value'])`, not robust to a correction for multiple tests), and its edge
  over the GBM is suggestive but not established on this test set.
- Watch for **multiple comparisons**, for choices made on the test set, and
  for the difference between **statistical and practical** significance.
